rows.explanation: The psalmist calls his days a declining shadow and himself withered grass, joining the waning day to a life running out.
Harvest and summer have ended and “we are not saved,” making a closing season the figure of missed rescue.
The day draws toward evening and grows to its end, a literal counterpart to asr as the day’s closing edge.
The disappearing day and stretched evening shadows turn late light into an urgent warning.
A thousand years shrink to yesterday or a night-watch before God, closely matching the conversion of a long age into a small part of a day.
It explicitly sets one day and a thousand years against each other before the Lord, matching the same reversal of temporal scale.
A raised-hand oath by the eternal God specifies “a time, times, and an half,” making solemn swearing explicitly about measured time.
The angel swears and says that there will be no more time or delay, an eschatological counterpart to time at its terminal edge.
It promises light at evening, reversing the late day’s normal movement into darkness.
It promises that the sun will no longer go down, the eschatological reverse of a declining day.
Jesus must work while it is day because a night comes when no one can work, making fading daylight a deadline for action.
The speaker’s age departs like a tent and his life is cut off, closely matching time as a life at its diminishing end.
Human life is a vapour that appears briefly and vanishes, matching asr’s compressed and fleeting side.
The acceptable time and day of salvation are declared to be now, answering the pressure of limited time with immediate response.
The unready brides arrive after the bridegroom and find the door shut, a scene of decisive loss through lateness.
Jerusalem’s destruction follows its failure to know the time of visitation, directly linking an unrecognized moment to loss.
Gaining the whole world while losing one’s soul states the human loss that makes worldly accumulation futile.
The saints are marked by patience, keeping God’s commandments, and faith, closely matching faith, righteous action, and patience together.
It says faith without works is dead, closely matching the conjunction of belief and righteous action.
Continuing to do good without weariness brings reaping in due season, joining deeds, patience, and time.
The farmer waits patiently for precious fruit and the rains, combining patience with the timed crop-and-rain image.
Believers are told to speak truth each to a neighbour, a direct counterpart to mutual counsel in truth.
Believers are to exhort one another daily while it is called Today, combining mutual counsel with time’s urgency.
Mutual exhortation is intensified as the Day approaches, joining communal counsel to a closing temporal horizon.
Joseph is put in the king’s prison, matching the confinement from which the wine-presser’s restoration and long wait are read.
The imprisoned cupbearer presses grapes into Pharaoh’s cup, directly matching the prison dream of pressing wine.
The interpretation restores the cupbearer to serving Pharaoh, as the wine-presser is restored to serving his master.
The restored cupbearer forgets Joseph, matching the forgotten plea that prolongs Joseph’s prison wait.
Pharaoh’s dream arrives only after two full years, mirroring the extended interval after Joseph is forgotten.
The dream’s good cattle and ears are interpreted as seven years, matching a divinely disclosed time-plan.
It announces seven years of great plenty, the first phase of the same storage calendar.
It follows abundance with seven famine years that erase its memory, matching hard years after plenty.
Food is to be stored against famine, closely matching grain protected through lean years.
Workers make oil and tread winepresses yet suffer thirst, joining pressing with dry deprivation.
It explicitly treats forceful pressing as a process that brings something out, from butter and blood to strife.
Giving is pictured as a measure pressed down, shaken together, and running over, like pressure that releases abundance.
Seasonal rain yields grain, wine, and oil, directly matching the rain-to-produce sequence.
The clouds pour down rain abundantly upon humankind, closely matching the image of rain released from clouds.
Rain descends and makes earth bring forth seed and bread, matching the chain from water to fertile growth.
Earth drinks rain and produces useful herbs, corresponding to rain yielding productive growth.
A thirsty child’s tongue cleaves to the roof of its mouth, closely matching the image of a dry tongue.
God answers the thirsty whose tongue fails by giving water, reversing the dry-tongue outcome.
The thirsty are invited to come and drink, matching water as a means of rescue from desperate need.
The redeemed will thirst no more, exactly reversing the image of thirst and dryness.
Scattering can increase while withholding more than is right leads to poverty, matching the contrast between releasing and merely holding.
The people curse one who withholds corn and bless one who releases it for sale, directly paralleling hoarded produce and its moral reversal.
The command not to harden the heart or shut the hand against the poor directly answers the image of a hand that only holds.
The command to open the hand wide to the poor makes release rather than restraint the proper use of possession.
The vineyard’s gleanings must be left for poor people and strangers, reversing the garden owners’ intent to exclude them.
Grape gleanings must remain for the stranger, fatherless, and widow, reversing a harvest kept entirely from the needy.
The rich man plans larger barns to hold all his fruits and goods, closely matching accumulation that refuses release.
His life is required that night, turning stored abundance into the very loss that exposes its futility.
Fruit-withholding vineyard tenants lose the vineyard to others who will render its fruit, closely matching garden, withheld produce, and dispossession.
One who sees a needy brother but shuts up compassion embodies the grasp that holds rather than gives.
The Lord is called a refuge for the oppressed in times of trouble, directly matching refuge found under pressure.
The speaker takes refuge under God’s wings until calamities pass over, making shelter a place through which danger and time pass.
God is a refuge from storm and a shadow from heat, closely matching shelter against crushing external force.
The people are told to enter chambers and hide for a little moment until indignation passes, closely matching refuge that encloses a span of time.
A man is a hiding place from wind, a covert from tempest, and water in a dry place, combining shelter, storm, and thirst.
Believers are described as having fled for refuge, directly matching rescue through taking hold of a shelter.
The psalmist asks for his soul to be brought out of prison, matching confinement as a condition from which rescue is sought.
The good news includes liberty for captives and opening the prison to those bound, matching release from holding confinement.
The woman flees to a God-prepared place and is fed for a measured 1,260 days, closely paralleling refuge enclosing long time.
Sowing wind and reaping whirlwind makes a destructive storm the ripened consequence of human action.
The ruined vineyard is denied rain from the clouds, closely matching garden devastation through withdrawn fertility.
Ground that bears thorns after rain is rejected and ends in burning, matching the contrast between fruitful yield and dry residue.
The unfruitful branch withers and is gathered for fire, closely matching the dry remainder that follows failed fruitfulness.
The ripe harvest, full winepress, and overflowing vats become images of ripened wickedness and judgment.
The gathered vine of earth is cast into the great winepress of God’s wrath, using pressing as an image of final judgment.
A moving figure rises like pillars of smoke, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense, closely matching scent billowing upward behind one who passes.
It replaces sweet smell with stench, reversing the commentary’s image of a fragrant trace rising behind a person.
Seedtime and harvest, summer and winter, day and night are set as enduring cycles, supporting asr as time in its full recurring breadth.
The prayer to number our days answers limited human time with wisdom.
The psalmist asks to know his end and the measure of his days, closely matching reflection on life as a measured span.
Humanity flees like a shadow and does not continue, echoing the shrinking, departing side of time.
Every purpose has its season and time, paralleling asr as more than one clock-hour and as a comprehensive temporal order.
Remembering the Creator before evil days arrive makes youth and late life a narrowing moral opportunity.
The darkening of sun, light, moon, and stars turns the fading day into an image of old age.
God determines appointed times and the bounds of human dwelling, paralleling asr as an era with a measured limit.
The vision has an appointed time and may seem to tarry, directly engaging delay, waiting, and an arriving end.
Redeeming the time because the days are evil closely matches urgency within a diminishing span.
The night is far spent and the day is at hand, reversing the direction of the late-day image toward approaching light.
Releasing what is withheld into God’s storehouse is answered by opened heavens and overflowing blessing, joining giving and outpoured abundance.
Gideon threshes wheat by a winepress to hide it from oppressors, combining grain, a pressing-place, and protective concealment.
People tread olives and make wine yet do not enjoy oil or wine, matching labour, pressing, and loss of the expected yield.
The threshing floor and winepress fail to feed the people and new wine fails, reversing the expected abundance of pressing.
Treading the winepress alone turns the image of pressing into one of overwhelming judgment.
Waterless clouds carried by winds and fruitless withered trees reverse the rain-bearing cloud and fruitful-garden imagery.
God promises to carry and deliver people even to old age, answering the exposed weakness of life’s late stage.
The outward person perishes while the inward person is renewed day by day, answering physical decline with inward renewal.
God spreads the savour of knowledge in every place, paralleling the image of a beneficent fragrance that rises and remains.
The waters have come into the psalmist’s soul, paralleling the reversed image in which water itself becomes choking danger.
It says the end is near and the days are fulfilled, an explicit picture of time reaching its last edge.
Human days are a handbreadth and human age is nothing before God, matching time as a severely limited span.
Human days are like grass and a field flower, closely matching life read through fading natural time.
The wind passes over the flower and it is gone, matching the sudden disappearance of what seemed to endure.
Jesus commands walking while light remains before darkness overtakes, closely matching the urgency of a waning day.
Seeking the Lord while he may be found makes the available moment a limited opportunity.
God causes the sun to go down at noon and darkens the earth in clear day, intensifying the image of daylight abruptly lost.
The devil acts with great wrath because he knows that his time is short, making brief time a source of pressure.
There will be no night because God gives perpetual light, reversing the movement from afternoon toward darkness.
“Except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish” gives a general loss with an explicitly stated exception.
The verse identifies the patience and faith of the saints, closely matching the surah’s conjunction of faith and patience.
Love is to be enacted in deed and truth rather than merely spoken, joining righteous action with truth.
During the seven plentiful years the land produces abundantly, matching the first stage of Joseph’s timed abundance.
Joseph gathers food from the seven good years and stores it in the cities, matching preservation through approaching scarcity.
The seven plentiful years come to an end, marking the calendar’s turn from abundance to lack.
The seven famine years begin as predicted, closely matching the arrival of hard years after stored plenty.
God waters the earth, enriches it, and prepares grain, directly matching rain released into fertility.
The former and latter rains are given, closely matching the cloud-and-rain side of pressing imagery.
Floors fill with wheat and vats overflow with wine and oil, matching the abundance that follows rain and pressing.
The Lord makes clouds and gives showers and grass, directly matching rain-bearing clouds that yield growth.
Barns fill with plenty and presses burst out with new wine, matching released abundance from gathered produce.
The expected yield from a winepress is sharply reduced, matching pressing as an image of loss rather than bounty.
Hungry and thirsty people faint in soul, closely matching dry deprivation under pressure.
God satisfies the longing soul and fills the hungry soul with goodness, reversing the state of deprivation.
The parched ground becomes a pool and thirsty land springs of water, reversing dryness into sustained life.
The water Jesus gives becomes an enduring spring and prevents thirst, reversing the threatened dry outcome.
The thirsty receive freely from the fountain of the water of life, reversing thirst through an inexhaustible gift.
The tormented man asks for water to cool his tongue, closely matching a tongue consumed by thirst and heat.
Giving to the poor prevents lack while hiding one’s eyes brings curses, matching the contrast between release and withholding.
Giving food to the hungry and drink to the thirsty makes generosity toward need a decisive moral act.
The owner prepares a vineyard with a winepress but receives wild grapes, closely matching cultivated fruitfulness turned into disappointment.
A blessing within a cluster leads to the command not to destroy it, matching fruit preserved because it contains future good.
A fig tree stands fruitless in a vineyard through measured years, joining time, cultivation, and threatened loss.
The tree receives one further interval to bear fruit before being cut down, making delayed fruitfulness a final opportunity.
A shelter provides shade by day and refuge from storm and rain, directly combining time, protection, and weather.
Seeking the Lord may result in being hidden in the day of his anger, matching refuge from pressing danger.
Jesus would gather Jerusalem under his wings as a hen gathers chicks, but its refusal reverses the movement into refuge.
God brings prisoners out of darkness and breaks their bonds, matching release from constraining confinement.
A visitation comes with tempest, storm, and devouring flame, closely matching the destructive fiery whirlwind image.
The Lord’s wrath goes forth as a grievous whirlwind, matching storm as an instrument of devastating judgment.
A gift is called an odour of sweet smell, joining generous release with a pleasing lingering fragrance.
The heavenly lights mark seasons, days, and years, supporting asr as time in its widest ordered sense.
“My times are in thy hand” treats a life’s changing periods as a held and measured whole.
Human days have fixed bounds that cannot be passed, matching time as a constraining limit.
Work must be done now because the grave holds no work or knowledge, making present time a closing opportunity.
Gathering in summer is wisdom while sleeping in harvest is shame, matching time-sensitive work before the season closes.
The time is fulfilled and the kingdom is at hand, presenting a decisive moment that demands response.
Times and seasons belong to the Father’s authority, treating historical periods as divinely fixed.
The end of all things is at hand, making sober action the answer to a nearing temporal end.
Believers teach and admonish one another, closely matching mutual counsel within a faithful community.
Paul praises faith and patience amid persecutions, preserving the surah’s pairing in a trial-setting.
Patience is needed to receive the promise after doing God’s will, joining endurance to faithful action.
Patience is to complete its work, making endurance productive rather than merely passive.
The wicked must drain the dregs of the Lord’s cup, using wrung-out liquid as an image of judgment.
Those who plant pleasant vineyards will not drink their wine, matching the loss of fruit one expected to enjoy.
Waters surround the speaker even to the soul, matching the inverted image in which water itself becomes choking danger.
Wishing needy people well without giving necessities exposes the emptiness of withheld help.
The whirlwind scatters people like chaff and a rolling thing, matching the storm’s power to lift and disperse what stood on the ground.
Rain, floods, and winds strike a house until it falls, matching a storm that suddenly destroys accumulated security.
Christ’s self-giving offering is a sweet-smelling savour, paralleling fragrance as the trace of a beneficent act.
